parts: Lesson 8: Communicable and Life Style Diseases — Summary

Disease is a state of discomfort in which the normal functioning of the body is affected; each disease has its own signs and symptoms. White blood cells make antibodies that fight germs; the ability of the body to resist a particular disease is immunity.

Communicable (infectious) diseases spread from one person to another and are caused by germs and parasites (influenza, polio, typhoid, measles, mumps, chickenpox, tuberculosis, STIs and AIDS). The gap between entry of germs and the first symptoms is the incubation period; during it the person looks healthy but is a carrier. Modes of spread: food and water (unhygienic preparation, dirty hands and utensils, houseflies; typhoid, cholera, hepatitis, diarrhoea); air (influenza, conjunctivitis, mumps; crowded and poorly ventilated places); contact – direct (touching, sexual contact) or indirect (comb, towel, cup, glass); insects (flies and cockroaches carry germs; mosquito bite causes malaria, dengue, Japanese encephalitis).

Prevention: keep the patient's belongings separate; keep water in clean covered containers and boil drinking water and milk; cover all food; avoid cut fruits and vegetables sold uncovered; wash utensils; wash hands before cooking and eating and after the toilet; keep house well-ventilated; avoid crowds in an epidemic; personal hygiene; clean surroundings, covered drains, wire mesh on doors and windows, sanitary latrines; no spitting and cover the mouth when coughing; complete vaccination of children.

Cholera (food and water): severe watery diarrhoea like rice water, vomiting, cramps in legs, thirst; give plenty of fluids and ORS. Typhoid (food and water; symptoms after about 14–21 days): severe headache, fever with low pulse, dry white-coated tongue; blood tests and prescribed medicine. Hepatitis/jaundice (food and water; 20–35 days): fever, dark yellow urine, yellow eyes, paleness, loss of appetite; carbohydrate-rich diet and bed rest. Influenza (air; 1–3 days): fever, cold, cough, headache, body ache; control fever, steam inhalation. Tuberculosis (air; 4–6 days in the text table): persistent cough, loss of weight and appetite, weakness, rapid pulse, chest pain; calcium-rich diet, treatment regulated for one year. Malaria (mosquito bite; 10–14 days): fever with alternating chill and perspiration, headache; blood test. Tetanus (wound exposed to dust or rusted item; 4 days to 2 weeks): stiff neck, difficulty in chewing and swallowing, spasm of jaw and face muscles, back bent like a bow; isolate, wash wounds, place a ball of cotton between teeth. Pertussis or whooping cough (air; 7–12 days): bouts of cough with a whoop-like sound.

ORS: mix the packet in clean water only (no milk, juice or sugar); if unavailable, add 8 teaspoons of sugar and 1 teaspoon of salt to 1 litre of clean drinking water. In caring for the sick: consult the doctor early, give medicines on time, balanced diet, rest, clean room and clothes.

HIV (Human Immuno Deficiency Virus) attacks the body's defence system; when it is destroyed, AIDS (Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome) sets in. It spreads by sexual contact with an infected person, infected blood or body fluids (transfusion), infected needles and from infected mother to child during pregnancy or birth. It does not spread by shaking hands, kissing on the cheek, sharing toilet seats, standing close, sneezing or coughing, cups, plates, water or food. There is no cure or vaccine; prevention: one partner, protection, sterilised needles, tested blood from registered blood banks. HIV infection and AIDS are not the same; a nutritious diet and healthy lifestyle can delay AIDS.

Life style (non-communicable) diseases such as obesity, diabetes, hypertension and heart disease are chronic, do not spread from person to person and arise from faulty eating and living habits. They are common now in developing countries and in the productive age group, reduce productivity and are a lifelong financial burden; they can be prevented and controlled, not cured. Modifiable factors: food habits, physical activity, smoking and drinking, stress; non-modifiable: age and heredity. Causes: fast and junk food, processed and packed food, soft drinks replacing milk, use of vehicles and machines instead of walking, smoking, alcohol, stress. Prevention: regular exercise (walking, yoga, cycling), use stairs, balanced diet at proper times without overeating, avoid processed and packaged foods, eat whole grains and millets rather than refined foods, 400–500 g of fruits and vegetables a day, plenty of water, yoga and meditation, no smoking or alcohol, less TV and more outdoor activity.
